cards.explanation: The answer is the king. The writer says his heart is stirred by a noble theme as he recites his verses to the king, and his tongue is "…the pen of a skillful writer." (Psalm 45:1) A tongue that works like a pen. Mine works more like a smudge, and I'm the one holding the stamp.

The answer is True. The writer tells the king, "therefore God has blessed you forever." (Psalm 45:2) That's a long blessing, friends. I've had cookies that didn't last till dinner, so forever sounds WILD to me.
The answer is warrior. The writer says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) A sword at his side and a title like that. That's a warrior, friends.

The answer is False. The text says, "Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king’s foes; the nations fall beneath your feet." (Psalm 45:5) No one is driving the king back here. The nations are the ones who end up under his feet.

The answer is justice. The writer says, "…justice is the scepter of Your kingdom." (Psalm 45:6) A scepter is what a king holds, and this king holds justice. That tells you a lot about how this kingdom runs.

The answer is that he loved righteousness and hated wickedness. The psalm says, "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you above your companions with the oil of joy." (Psalm 45:7) The word therefore ties the two together, friends. The joy follows the love of what's right.
The answer is glad. The writer says, "from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad." (Psalm 45:8) Harps, ivory palaces, and fragrance everywhere. That's a whole mood, friends.
The answer is the queen. The writer says, "the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir." (Psalm 45:9) She's at his right hand, dressed in gold. Gold of Ophir, no less.

The answer is that the king will desire her beauty. The writer says, "Forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:10-11) Notice who's doing the desiring: the king. That's a lot of attention for one song. I'd be blushing under this mustache.

The answer is favor. The writer says, "men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) Rich men lining up just to get on her good side. When I want a neighbor's favor, I show up at the door with a warm batch of cookies.
The answer is king. The text says, "In colorful garments she is led to the king…" (Psalm 45:14) Every step of this song heads toward the king. Colorful garments, too, and I'm a rainbow fan myself.

The answer is False. The song says, "They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king." (Psalm 45:15) Joy and gladness, not fear and trembling. Walk in like that and even the doors would smile.

The answer is True. The writer says, "Your sons will succeed your fathers; you will make them princes throughout the land." (Psalm 45:16) Princes throughout the land, no less. That's a lot of royal titles to hand out.

The answer is praise. The writer says, "therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever." (Psalm 45:17) Because the name is remembered, the praise keeps going. Forever and ever is a long time to keep a song going.
